title: A feature check builds one operation on a simple shape, so the right answer is known before you look
summary: Each small plot applies one modelling operation (fillet, circular pattern, revolve, shell, circular sweep) to a simple primitive whose correct result can be stated in a sentence, for example revolve of a rectangle is an annulus and a circular sweep of a disc is a torus. The check is: does the picture match the sentence in its title?

source.caption: Feature check (plot, 440 px): revolve(rectangle) = annulus
source.note: Representative figure: revolve(rectangle) = annulus. Seven small 440 px plots, two of them top views. The plots print no numbers apart from axis ticks; no volumes or tolerances are shown.
group: 114_verify_pattern_circular: Feature check (plot, 440 px): circular pattern x5
115_verify_pattern_circular_top: Feature check (plot, 440 px): circular pattern x5, top view
118_verify_sweep_torus: Feature check (plot, 440 px): circular sweep = torus
119_verify_sweep_torus_top: Feature check (plot, 440 px): circular sweep = torus, top view

read_the_figure.question: Does the operation named in the title produce the shape that the operation is defined to produce?
read_the_figure.axes: A small 3D view with plain x, y, z ticks (about -1.5 to 1.5 for the revolve plot; about -2 to 2 for the fillet and pattern plots; about -3 to 3 for the torus top view). The title is the claim: 'revolve(rectangle) = annulus'. The axes are not equal-aspect in the oblique views, so spheres can look like ellipsoids: use the tick labels, not the apparent roundness.
look_at: Revolve: a rectangle placed away from the axis revolved about it. Expect a ring of rectangular cross-section, a thick-walled tube: outer wall, a visible inner wall and an open centre. The figure shows exactly that, with a hole through the middle.

Shell: a hollow sphere of wall thickness t = 0.3. From outside it looks like a plain sphere; the wall is only visible in a cut-away or a section, and this view does not give one. Treat it as unverified by eye.

Fillet of two spheres: expect a smooth bridge where the two bodies come close. In the oblique view the two bodies appear separated; a bridge is not visible, so this plot alone does not confirm the fillet.

Circular pattern x5: five copies of a sphere equally spaced on a circle. The top view is the best test: five spheres at equal angular spacing about the origin, which is what is drawn (one at angle 0, the others at 72, 144, 216, 288 degrees).
Circular sweep = torus: a disc swept around a circle. The top view shows an annulus: outer edge, inner hole, constant ring width all the way round.
read_the_figure.proves: That the operation behaves correctly on a case whose answer is known exactly: the topology is right (a hole where there should be one, five copies where five were asked for) and the symmetry is right (equal spacing, constant ring width). Top views turn a symmetry claim into something you can check against a ruler.
if_wrong: Revolve: a filled disc-like cylinder instead of a ring means the profile touched the axis or the revolve axis was wrong; a missing end cap or inner wall means the profile was open.
Pattern: copies not evenly spaced or fewer than five means the angular step or the count is wrong; copies drifting off the circle means the pattern centre is not where assumed.
Sweep: a ring that is not constant in width means the sweep path or the profile orientation is wrong; a cut ring means an angle shorter than 360 degrees.
Shell: a solid sphere has not been hollowed; to test, look at a section or compute volume.
Fillet: separate bodies with no bridge means the fillet did nothing, or the radius is smaller than the gap.
must_check: A view in which the claim can actually be seen: a section for shell, a view into the gap for fillet, a top view for patterns and sweeps.
Equal-aspect axes, or an explicit statement that they are not.
A quantitative companion: volume against a formula (annulus, torus, shell), count of copies, and the angle between neighbours.
The parameters behind the title (radii, thickness, angle) printed, not only the title.

terms.meaning: Sweep a planar profile through an angle (here 360 degrees) around an axis. A rectangle off the axis gives a ring; a semicircle on the axis gives a sphere.
The region between an inner and an outer radius. Revolving a rectangle gives a thick-walled tube with circular cross-section outline.
Hollow a solid, keeping a wall of thickness t. For a sphere of radius R the wall lies between radii R - t and R.
A rounding that blends two surfaces or bodies smoothly, with a radius that sets how much material is added or removed.
n copies of a feature, each rotated by 360/n degrees about an axis.
Sweep a profile along a circular path. A disc of radius r along a circle of radius R gives a torus.
A view along the z axis. It removes depth, so symmetry in the xy-plane can be judged directly.
A test of one operation on an input with a known exact answer, as opposed to a cross-check of whole engines.

remember: A feature check is only as good as the sentence in its title: choose cases whose answer you can state exactly.
Revolve volume: V = 2 pi times the profile's centroid distance times its area (Pappus). For a rectangle of width w and height H from radius r1: V = pi (r2^2 - r1^2) H.
n equal copies on a circle are 360/n degrees apart: five copies are 72 degrees apart.
Torus volume: 2 pi^2 R r^2; shell volume: 4/3 pi (R^3 - (R - t)^3).
A picture shows topology and symmetry, not volume. Pair each check with a number.
understand: These seven plots are the small, fast layer of a test pyramid: single operations on a primitive. The 45-figure cross-engine group is the larger layer: whole shapes through different kernels. A bug found at the feature level is far easier to localise.
Two of the seven are top views of plots that already have an oblique view. They exist because the oblique view cannot show equal spacing or constant ring width.

steps.title: Revolve a rectangle: Pappus and direct integration agree
steps.note: Washer integration gives the first form; Pappus's centroid theorem gives the second. They are the same because (r2^2 - r1^2) = (r2 - r1)(r1 + r2). Checked symbolically.

steps.title: Circular pattern
steps.note: With n = 5 the angular step is 72 degrees. In the top view the five sphere centres are the vertices of a regular pentagon of circumradius rho.

steps.title: Circular sweep gives a torus
steps.note: u runs around the big circle, v around the disc. Top view: the radial distance rho = R + r cos v ranges from R - r to R + r, an annulus.

steps.title: Torus volume
steps.note: Pappus again: the disc's area times the distance its centroid travels.

steps.title: Shell volume
steps.note: Outer ball minus inner ball. For small t it approaches the surface area times thickness, 4 pi R^2 t, which is a useful sanity limit.

steps.title: A fillet in the field
steps.note: One common way to blend two bodies when they are described by distance fields: a smooth minimum. A B-rep kernel instead inserts a rolling-ball surface. Either way the test is whether a bridge appears between the bodies.

worked.title: What should the shell figure contain?
worked.problem: Illustrative: a sphere of radius R = 1 hollowed with wall thickness t = 0.3 (the title gives t; the radius here is assumed). What volume should a correct shell have, and what would the solid sphere have?
worked.answer: A correct shell holds about 66 percent of the solid sphere's volume (0.657). The picture cannot show this; a volume or a section does.

analyze.q: In the fillet plot the two bodies look like separate ellipsoids. Give two different explanations (one about the plot, one about the operation) and say how to tell them apart.
analyze.hint: Axis aspect, and a view into the gap.

analyze.q: Why does a top view settle a question that the oblique pattern view cannot?
A revolve check shows a ring with no inner wall visible. List what could cause it.

evaluate.q: Which of the five checks, as plotted, actually verify their title, and which do not? What would you add?
evaluate.hint: Revolve and the top views do; shell and fillet need sections or numbers.

evaluate.q: Are visual feature checks enough to trust a modelling kernel?
evaluate.hint: Think of tolerance, edge cases and automated assertions.

create: Turn each feature check into an automated test: for each of the five operations, write the assertion (a volume formula, a count, an angle) that replaces the visual judgement.
Design a section view for the shell and a close-up for the fillet so that both claims become visible.

checks.q: Why choose revolve(rectangle) as a test case?
checks.answer: Because its result, a thick-walled ring, and its volume pi (r2^2 - r1^2) H are known exactly, so any deviation is a bug rather than a matter of opinion.

checks.q: Five copies are placed evenly on a circle. What is the angle between neighbours, and the chord length for circle radius 1?
The torus top view shows a ring whose width is the same all round. What does that confirm, and what does it not?
checks.hint: Think about what the top view hides.
checks.answer: It confirms the sweep is circular and the disc keeps its size along the path. It does not confirm the disc is round in the vertical direction or the volume; the oblique view and 2 pi^2 R r^2 do.

checks.q: A shell figure looks like a solid sphere. Is the shell broken?
checks.answer: Not necessarily: the wall is inside and invisible from outside. It is unverified, not failed. A section or a volume check decides.

checks.q: Propose a feature check for a taper operation.
checks.hint: Pick a primitive with a known result.
checks.answer: Taper a cylinder: the cross-section radius should vary linearly with height, so the result is a conical frustum with volume (pi h / 3)(R^2 + R r + r^2). Plot a section and compare the volume to the formula.
